props.title: Where the Sidewalk Ends

sections.content: Where the Sidewalk Ends (1950) stands as Otto Preminger's darker companion piece to his earlier noir masterpiece Laura (1944). Both films star Dana Andrews as a detective, but here he's transformed into Mark Dixon, a brutal cop whose violence stems from a desperate need to distance himself from his criminal father's legacy. The film exemplifies noir's postwar pessimism, sharing thematic DNA with The Big Heat (1953) and On Dangerous Ground (1951) in its exploration of police brutality and redemption.

sections.content: Preminger's direction is a masterclass in noir style, using deep shadows and canted angles to externalize Dixon's psychological torment. The film's Greenwich Village setting provides a grimy, claustrophobic atmosphere that contrasts sharply with the more glamorous Manhattan locations of Laura (1944). Gene Tierney returns as a Preminger leading lady, but her Morgan Taylor is working-class, adding to the film's stark realism. The screenplay by Ben Hecht (uncredited) and Victor Trivas twists conventional noir tropes by making the cop, not the criminal, the moral center of corruption. SUBHEAD: Visual Style and Technical Innovation

The film's cinematography by Joseph LaShelle deserves special attention. Having won an Oscar for Laura (1944), LaShelle brings similar technical virtuosity but with a grittier edge. His use of location shooting predates the better-known street photography of The Naked City (1948), creating a documentary-like immediacy that influenced later police dramas like The French Connection (1971). The interrogation scenes, with their harsh overhead lighting, became a template for noir cinematography.
